title: Do Architects in Westchester Handle Permits? Yes, and Here's Why That Matters
excerpt: When you hire an architect for your Westchester home project, permit handling shouldn't be a separate headache. Here's what you need to know about working with someone who knows the local process inside and out.
content:
If you're planning a home renovation in Westchester County, you've probably wondered who actually handles all those permits. The answer is straightforward: yes, a licensed architect in Westchester, NY should absolutely be managing your permits. But there's a catch. Not all architects do, and that's where things get messy.

Permits aren't optional paperwork you can skip over. Every municipality in Westchester has its own building department and review process. Whether you're working on a project in Scarsdale, Bronxville, or Mamaroneck, you need someone who understands how that specific town works and can shepherd your plans through approval.

Why Your Architect Should Handle Permits

When an architect prepares drawings for your project, they're already working to code. They know what the building department will ask for. So it makes sense for the same person to submit those plans and answer questions as they come up.

If you hire your architect and your contractor separately, you end up playing phone tag between two people who don't talk to each other. One blames the other when something gets flagged. You're stuck in the middle, frustrated and confused. That's not how it should work.

A design-build approach in Westchester solves this problem. When your architect is also your general contractor, or when they work as a true team, permits become one less thing you have to worry about. The same person responsible for your plans is responsible for getting them approved. There's accountability built in.

Every Town Has Its Own Process

Westchester is made up of dozens of municipalities, and they all run their building departments a little differently. White Plains has different requirements than Rye. Larchmont's review timeline isn't the same as Hastings-on-Hudson's. This isn't a flaw in the system. It's just how local government works.

What matters is that your architect knows these differences and knows who to call when something isn't clear. Someone with roots in the county, who has worked with these building departments for years, knows the shortcuts and the pitfalls. They know which inspectors ask detailed questions and how to prepare accordingly.

For example, home additions in Westchester often require architectural review at the municipal level, especially in towns like Pelham and Tuckahoe. An experienced local architect builds that timeline into the project plan from day one. You're not caught off guard waiting three months for a decision.

What It Looks Like When Your Architect Owns the Process

At House Architecture and Construction, Silvio Luca is both a licensed architect in New York and a licensed general contractor. He runs every project personally. When he's designing your kitchen remodel in Pelham Manor or your second-story addition in Eastchester, he's already thinking about permits. He prepares the drawings with the building department in mind. He submits them. He responds to questions. He coordinates with the inspector during construction.

That continuity matters. It keeps your project on track. It prevents misunderstandings between design and construction. And it means you're not paying multiple people to do overlapping work.
